title: Pressure and pressure differences in fluids (physics only)

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Pascal
items.clue: One newton acting on each square metre.

items.label: Atmosphere
items.clue: The thin layer of air around the Earth.

items.label: Fluid
items.clue: A substance that can flow: a liquid or a gas.

questions.stem: In physics, what is meant by the term 'fluid'?

options.text: A substance that can flow: a liquid or a gas.
A liquid only, since a gas cannot be poured.
Anything that pours, such as dry sand.
A gas only, as gases fill any space.

questions.explanation: The specification states that a fluid can be either a liquid or a gas; both can flow and both exert pressure.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a simple model of the Earth's atmosphere?

options.text: A deep layer of gas that gets denser as altitude rises.
A thick layer of air of the same density at all heights.
A layer of air about as deep as the Earth is wide.
A thin layer of air round the Earth that thins with altitude.

questions.explanation: The specification describes a thin layer, relative to the size of the Earth, that gets less dense with altitude.

questions.stem: A sealed can holds compressed air. In which direction does the air pressure exert a force on the flat top of the can?

options.text: Vertically downwards, pulled by the air's weight.
At right angles to the top, pushing outwards.
Sideways across the top, following the airflow.
Inwards to the centre of the sealed can.

questions.explanation: The pressure in a fluid causes a force normal to any surface it touches.

questions.stem: Explain why atmospheric pressure at the top of a mountain is lower than at sea level.

options.text: Gravity is much weaker at the top of a high mountain.
The air up there is colder, so it presses down less hard.
There is less air above, so fewer molecules collide.
The wind is stronger high up, blowing the air away.

questions.explanation: Fewer air molecules above the surface means less weight of air and fewer collisions with it.

questions.stem: Water in a reservoir presses on a sloping side wall. How does the force from the water act on that wall?

options.text: Vertically downwards all the way down the wall.
Straight downwards, in line with the water's weight.
Normal to the wall at every point along it.
Along the wall, the way the water runs.

questions.explanation: Pressure in a fluid causes a force at right angles to the surface, whatever its angle.

questions.stem: Which equation gives the pressure at the surface of a fluid?

options.text: pressure = (area of that surface)/(force normal to that surface)
pressure = (force normal to a surface) × (area of the surface)
pressure = (force parallel to a surface)/(area of that surface)
pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface)

questions.explanation: This is the equation exactly as the specification states it: p = F/A.

questions.stem: A force of 4500 N acts at right angles to a surface of area 0.03 m². Calculate the pressure on the surface.

options.text: 135 Pa

questions.stem: A crate presses on the floor with a force of 2400 N normal to the floor and exerts a pressure of 800 Pa. Calculate the area of contact.

options.text: 3 m²
30 m²

questions.stem: In the equation p = F/A, what unit is the pressure p measured in?

options.text: Newton per metre, N/m.
Newtons, written N.
Square metres, m².
Pascals, written Pa.

questions.explanation: The specification gives pressure, p, in pascals, Pa.

questions.stem: A force of 16 N acts normal to a surface of area 200 cm². Calculate the pressure in pascals. 1 m² = 10 000 cm²

options.text: 8 Pa
80 Pa
800 Pa

questions.stem: A brick of mass 2.0 kg rests flat on a bench. gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg  Which value is the force normal to the bench in p = F/A?

options.text: 19.6 N, the weight of the brick.
2.0 N, the mass rewritten in newtons.
9.8 N, the field strength in N/kg.
0.20 N, the mass divided by g.

questions.explanation: F must be a force in newtons: weight = 2.0 x 9.8 = 19.6 N.

questions.stem: A walker on soft snow puts on wide snowshoes and stops sinking in. Why?

options.text: The larger area increases the pressure on the snow.
The larger area reduces the pressure on the snow.
The larger area presses down harder on the snow.
The force is the walker's mass, and wide shoes shrink it.

questions.explanation: The normal force is unchanged but is spread over more area, so p = F/A falls.

questions.stem: Which word equation gives the pressure due to a column of liquid?

options.text: pressure = width of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength
pressure = height of the column × area of the column × gravitational field strength
pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength
pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid / gravitational field

questions.explanation: This is the word equation exactly as the specification states it.

questions.stem: In the equation p = h ρ g, how is the height h of the liquid column found from the other quantities?

options.text: Multiply the pressure by ρ g.
Divide ρ g by the pressure value.
Subtract ρ g from the pressure.
Divide the pressure by ρ g.

questions.explanation: ρ and g multiply h in p = h ρ g, so h = p divided by ρ g.

questions.stem: In the equation p = h ρ g, which units must be used for p and for h?

options.text: p in pascals, Pa and h in centimetres, cm
p in pascals, Pa and h in metres, m
p in newtons, N and h in centimetres, cm
p in newtons, N and h in metres, m

questions.explanation: The specification gives pressure in pascals, Pa and height of the column in metres, m.

questions.stem: In the equation p = h ρ g, what unit must the density ρ be given in?

options.text: Kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³.
Kilograms per litre, kg/l.
Grams per centimetre cubed, g/cm³.
Newtons per metre cubed, N/m³.

questions.explanation: The specification gives density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³.

questions.stem: An exam question asks for the pressure at the bottom of a column of sea water. What does the specification say about the gravitational field strength g?

options.text: It must be recalled from memory as 9.8 N/kg.
It is measured in newtons, N, and is recalled.
It is always taken as exactly 10 N/kg here.
Its value will be given in the question, in N/kg.

questions.explanation: The specification states that in any calculation the value of g will be given.

questions.stem: Explain why the pressure at a point in a liquid increases as that point gets deeper.

options.text: The liquid becomes denser lower down, where it is squashed.
The liquid flows downwards, pressing harder low down.
A taller column of liquid lies above it, weighing more.
The container holds a lot more liquid low down than high up.

questions.explanation: Pressure is h ρ g: a greater height of liquid above the point means more weight above it.
